title: You Want Revival in the Church. Would You Still Want It If Revival Started With Your Repentance?
paragraphs: You Want Revival in the Church. Would You Still Want It If Revival Started With Your Repentance?
Everybody wants God to change the Church. The terrifying question is what happens when God answers by beginning with the person praying.

You have watched Christianity become comfortable where it should have been courageous. You have seen compromise dressed in Christian vocabulary. You have watched believers fight one another while barely fighting their own sin. You have watched churches become distracted, families fracture, secret addictions grow, prayer lives disappear, and people who once burned for Christ slowly learn how to survive on yesterday’s fire.
And somewhere inside you, a prayer rose:
But there is a question hidden inside that prayer that few of us want God to ask.
Not the person who offended you.
Not the hypocrite you cannot stand.
Not the denomination you think has compromised.
Not the lukewarm Christians you keep criticizing.
Would you still want revival if the first thing God revived was your conscience?
Would you still ask for fire if that fire illuminated the room in your heart where you have been hiding something?
Would you still cry, “Send revival,” if heaven answered, “Then bring Me your repentance”?
David prayed something astonishing near the end of Psalm 139.
Not, “God, show me what is wrong with everyone around me.”
He turned the searchlight toward himself.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.”
The Hebrew makes the prayer even more piercing.

חָקְרֵנִי אֵל וְדַע לְבָבִי
בְּחָנֵנִי וְדַע שַׂרְעַפָּי׃
וּרְאֵה אִם־דֶּרֶךְ־עֹצֶב בִּי
וּנְחֵנִי בְּדֶרֶךְ עוֹלָם׃
Chaqreni El, v’da levavi; bechaneni, v’da sar’appai. U’reh im-derekh-otsev bi, un’cheni b’derekh olam.
The Hebrew verb חָקַר (chaqar) carries the idea of searching out, examining, investigating.
David is essentially opening the locked doors.
Look beneath what people think about me.
Look beneath the version of myself I have learned to present.
Go where I do not want anyone else to go.
The underlying Hebrew verb בָּחַן (bachan) is used for testing or examining. David is not merely asking God to observe his behavior. He is inviting divine examination.
“See whether there is a grievous way in me.”
The expression דֶּרֶךְ־עֹצֶב (derekh-otsev) can carry the sense of a hurtful, grievous, or offensive way.
Notice where David locates the possibility.
That may be one of the hardest locations for a religious person to search.
We are often extraordinarily talented at detecting sin at a distance.
We can diagnose somebody else’s pride while protecting our own.
We can condemn somebody else’s sexual sin while quietly feeding lust.
We can preach forgiveness while maintaining a private museum of everything people have done to us.
We can sing about surrender while negotiating with God over the one thing we refuse to surrender.
We can post Scripture publicly and starve spiritually privately.
We can criticize churches for lacking prayer while barely praying ourselves.
We can complain that Christians have lost their first love while knowing that our own Bible has been sitting unopened for days.
We can speak passionately about holiness while carefully renaming the sins we enjoy.
Lust becomes “a struggle I’m working through” while we continue supplying it.
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, we become experts at wanting revival everywhere except the places where revival would hurt.
Because real revival is not merely emotional excitement.
It is not just a crowded altar.
It is not goosebumps during worship.
It is not a viral sermon clip.
It is not louder music, longer services, packed auditoriums, or Christians announcing that something historic is happening.
Those things may accompany genuine awakening, but they cannot define it.
Biblically, when God brings people back to Himself, sin cannot remain comfortably enthroned.
Jesus began His public proclamation with words our generation desperately needs to hear again:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
Not repent so God might finally decide to love you.
Not clean yourself up enough to earn Jesus.
Not punish yourself until God considers the debt settled.
The Gospel is far better than that.
The sinless Son of God bore sin on the cross.
And when grace truly arrests a human heart, it does not merely make us feel forgiven while leaving us content to remain unchanged.
Grace teaches us to come out of hiding.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance says, “Jesus, I cannot keep defending what You died to save me from.”
Maybe that is where revival begins.
Maybe you have been asking God to heal your marriage while refusing to repent of how cruel your words have become.
Maybe you have been asking God to save your children while they have watched you profess Christ publicly and live differently at home.
Maybe everyone at church thinks you are strong, but nobody knows what happens when the door closes and the screen lights up.
Maybe you have been wounded deeply, and somewhere along the way legitimate pain hardened into bitterness.
Maybe ministry became your identity and Jesus quietly stopped being your intimacy.
Maybe you know how to preach.
You know when to raise your hands.
You know exactly what to say when somebody asks how you are doing.
But underneath all of it, something has been dying.
There was a time when Scripture pierced you.
There was a time when sin grieved you.
There was a time when prayer was where you met God.
Now it is something you promise yourself you will restart tomorrow.
There was a time when Jesus was enough.
Now you need Jesus plus attention.
Jesus plus the secret thing nobody knows about.
And perhaps the most frightening part is not that you wandered.
It is that you learned how to look spiritually alive while wandering.
If the Spirit of God is exposing something in you right now, exposure does not have to become your funeral.
In Christ, it can become the doorway home.
Then, under pressure, he denied even knowing Him.
Imagine remembering your own voice saying, “I do not know the man.”
Imagine seeing the One you loved after discovering that when the moment came, your courage collapsed.
But Peter’s failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Not to tell Peter sin did not matter.
Jesus brought him face-to-face with love, allegiance, and calling.
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?”
And the man who had denied Christ would become a man who publicly proclaimed Christ.
Grace does not rewrite history by calling evil good.
Jesus rewrites people by redeeming sinners.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Maybe your scandal is not public.
Maybe there will never be headlines.
Maybe the scandal is happening silently inside your soul.
A dishonest businessman who quotes Bible verses.
A ministry leader addicted to being needed.
A believer secretly jealous when somebody else is blessed.
A Christian who knows how to defend doctrine but has forgotten how to love people.
A person who keeps saying, “God understands,” when what you really mean is, “I do not want to surrender this yet.”
Psalm 139 begins long before David asks God to search him.
“O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me.”
The God David invites to search him is the God who already knows him.
You are not confessing because heaven lacks evidence.
You are confessing because hiding has become useless.
And still Christ calls sinners to come.
You do not have to impress the One who already knows the worst thing about you.
You need to come to Him truthfully.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The answer to conviction is not self-hatred.
It is not performing religious punishment.
It is not announcing every private sin to the internet.
It is not trying to make yourself miserable enough to deserve mercy.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Stop feeding what is destroying you.
This is why revival becomes frightening when it becomes personal.
We love praying, “Lord, change the world.”
But perhaps tonight heaven is asking:
Will you let Me change you?
What if thousands of Christians stopped asking first, “What is wrong with the Church?” and began asking:
What if pastors prayed it before preaching it?
What if worship leaders prayed it before singing?
What if husbands prayed it before blaming their wives?
What if wives prayed it before listing everything their husbands need to change?
What if parents prayed it before correcting their children?
What if ministry leaders prayed it before planning the next conference?
What if the Christian who has spent years pointing at everyone else finally closed the door, fell before God, and whispered:
Revival becomes very different when the person asking for it stops volunteering everybody else.
And maybe this article reached you because there is something you already know.
Something God has been touching for months.
A person you need to forgive.
A person from whom you need to ask forgiveness.
Something you need to stop defending.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
The cross proves that sin is far more serious than our culture wants to admit.
The cross also proves that the mercy of God is more astonishing than repentant sinners dare to imagine.
So stop hiding behind the sentence, “But you don’t know what I’ve done.”
The question is not whether He knows.
The question is whether you will finally stop running from the One who does.
Maybe your revival prayer needs to become smaller tonight.
“Show me everything wrong with the Church.”
“See if there is any grievous way in me.”
David does not merely ask God to expose him.
He asks God to lead him.
God does not expose sin merely so we can sit in shame staring at ourselves.
He calls us away from sin and toward Himself.
The road does not end at your failure.
For those who come to Christ, there is grace on the other side of confession.
There is forgiveness on the other side of repentance.
There is restoration beyond the ruins.
There is a Savior standing where your self-salvation finally collapses.
So before you share another post about what is wrong with Christianity…
Before you complain again about the condition of the Church…
Before you ask God for another revival…
And do not pray it unless you are willing for God to answer.
“See if there is any grievous way in me.”
Do not rush past whatever the Spirit brings into the light.
Repentance is not measured by emotional intensity.
Maybe you have spent years pretending.
The same Gospel that exposes our inability to save ourselves announces the Savior who came for sinners.
This is where scandal meets grace.
This is where the prodigal stops rehearsing excuses and goes home.
This is where Peter discovers that denial does not have to have the last word.
This is where the hidden sinner steps into the light.
This is where the exhausted believer stops performing.
This is where the Christian who wanted revival for everybody else finally whispers:
You do not need to publish private details. God does not require public oversharing to prove repentance. But there is something powerful about refusing to pretend you need no grace.
Remind somebody that Christ still receives repentant sinners.
Come back to Psalm 139:23–24 when your heart begins making excuses again.
Not as an announcement that everybody else needs repentance.
Share it as your own prayer:

A shared Gospel message may reach the exhausted Christian who would never tell you they are struggling, the friend quietly drifting from Christ, the family member carrying secret shame, the lukewarm believer who has learned to survive without intimacy with God, or even the unbeliever who has never understood that Christianity is not about good people congratulating themselves.
It is about sinners needing a Savior.

We glorify God by faith in Christ expressed through lives surrendered to Him. But if this ministry is bearing biblical fruit in your life, voluntarily supporting it is one practical way you can help Gospel-centered messages continue reaching others.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, sharing, and putting Christ-centered resources into the hands of people who need them.
Seek help where help is needed.
Because perhaps the revival you have spent years asking God to send does not begin when everybody else finally gets serious.
Perhaps, for you, it begins tonight.
Just one human heart finally giving God permission to search the places it has spent years defending.
Remember this when you are tempted to pray for fire while protecting the darkness:
The revival you keep asking God to send may begin the moment you stop asking Him to change everyone else and finally let Jesus have all of you.
